project_name: Security and Privacy Requirements Analysis Tool
initial_requirements: Requirements and privacy analysts need SPRAT, a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies. Users should be able to capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and legal-compliance information; trace goals back to their source policies; organize them with flexible classifications; and compare analyses produced by different people. Access should vary for administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary goals and success criteria for SPRAT from the stakeholders’ perspective?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
From our perspective, SPRAT should make it much easier for analysts to connect security and privacy requirements back to the policies and legal obligations they came from, without losing traceability. It also needs to support collaboration, so different people can work on the same analysis, compare their results, and spot gaps or inconsistencies quickly.
We’d consider it successful if teams can produce more complete and consistent analyses in less time, with clear evidence of how each requirement was derived. Another big sign of success would be that people with different roles can use it appropriately, with access controlled in a way that protects sensitive information but doesn’t slow down the work.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What boundary conditions, exceptions, or special cases should SPRAT handle for the analysis process—for example, incomplete or conflicting source policies, missing legal obligations, partial analyses, or cases where traceability cannot be established?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Yes, those situations do come up, and SPRAT should handle them explicitly instead of forcing analysts to pretend everything is complete. If a source policy is incomplete or a legal obligation is missing, the system should let the analyst flag that gap, record assumptions, and mark the item as unresolved so it’s visible in the analysis.
For conflicting policies or requirements, SPRAT should allow both versions to be captured and highlight the conflict so a reviewer can resolve it later. And if traceability can’t be established for something, that should be treated as a documented exception, not silently ignored, so partial analyses are still usable and clearly labeled as partial.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When analysts compare or update analyses over time, how should SPRAT manage analysis versions—for example, should it keep full histories of changes, allow branching or merging, identify who changed what and when, and let users compare earlier versions side by side?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
We do need a full history of changes, because in practice people will want to see how an analysis evolved and who made each change. It should identify the user, the timestamp, and ideally the reason for the change if they provide one, since that helps with review and accountability.
Side-by-side comparison of earlier versions is important, especially for spotting differences in goals, requirements, or trace links. Branching and merging might be useful, but I’d treat that as a nice-to-have unless teams are working in parallel a lot; I’m not sure we need full version-control style workflows on day one.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When an analyst changes a goal, requirement, policy link, or other analysis item in SPRAT, what review and approval workflow should that change follow before it becomes visible or final—for example, should changes be immediately saved, require peer review, or need explicit approval from a project manager or administrator?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The change should be saved immediately so the analyst doesn’t lose work, but it shouldn’t always be considered final right away. For most edits, I’d expect a draft or pending state until a review happens, especially when the change affects traceability, policy interpretation, or legal compliance.
I think peer review should be the normal path, with project managers stepping in for anything higher risk or contentious, and administrators only handling access or system-level issues. The exact approval rule probably depends on the project’s configuration, because not every team will want the same level of control.

turns.interviewer_utterance: How should SPRAT manage the draft or pending state for changes after they are saved—for example, what actions are allowed while an item is still draft, what makes it transition to reviewed or final, and who can see or edit it at each stage?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
While something is in draft or pending, the analyst who created it should be able to keep editing it and probably withdraw or revise it before review. Other analysts and project managers should at least be able to see that it exists, but I’d expect visibility to be limited if the item contains sensitive material or has not been approved yet.
It should move to reviewed or final only after the required reviewer signs off, and that approval should be recorded in the history. Once it’s final, edits should create a new revision rather than overwriting the approved one, so the approved version stays intact for audit and comparison.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For items that are still in draft or pending review, what exactly should other roles be able to see or do, and what rules should determine when the item’s content, metadata, or existence is visible versus hidden because it is sensitive or not yet approved?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Other roles should usually be able to see that a draft exists, who owns it, what it is roughly about, and its review status, but not necessarily the full content if it’s sensitive or still under discussion. I’d expect project managers and assigned reviewers to see more detail than general analysts, while guests should probably see nothing about drafts unless a project explicitly allows it.
As a rule, the item’s existence and basic metadata can be visible to people with the right project access, but the content itself should be hidden until it is approved or explicitly shared. If an item is marked sensitive, then even the metadata may need to be limited to only the author, reviewers, and admins.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Which external tools, repositories, or upstream systems should SPRAT be able to import analysis data from, and what kinds of imported content or structure must be preserved during that import?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
We definitely expect SPRAT to import from common document sources and possibly spreadsheets or structured exports from other requirements tools, since a lot of analyses start outside the system. I’d also expect support for importing policy or compliance references from upstream repositories if the team already maintains those separately, but I’m not sure we’ve narrowed down the exact systems yet.
What matters most is preserving the structure of the analysis, not just the text, so goals, scenarios, requirements, policy links, and traceability need to come across intact. If there are classifications, tags, or version references in the source, those should be retained too where possible, though we may need to map them if the source format doesn’t match SPRAT exactly.

slots.name: project_goals
slots.value: Make it easier for analysts to connect security and privacy requirements back to their source policies and legal obligations while preserving traceability; support collaboration so multiple people can work on the same analysis, compare results, and identify gaps or inconsistencies; enable more complete and consistent analyses in less time with clear evidence of requirement derivation; provide role-based access that protects sensitive information without slowing work.

slots.name: stakeholder_roles
slots.value: Administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests; different roles should have appropriate access control.

slots.name: functional_needs
slots.value: Support collaborative analysis on the same project, compare analyses from different people, trace requirements back to source policies and legal obligations, manage role-based access to sensitive information, flag missing policies or legal obligations, record assumptions, capture conflicting policies or requirements, mark unresolved or partial analyses as visible exceptions, keep a full history of analysis changes with user, timestamp, and optional reason, and support side-by-side comparison of earlier versions.

slots.name: business_rules
slots.value: Requirements and goals must remain traceable to their originating policies and legal obligations; access must be controlled according to user role so sensitive information is protected; analyses from different people should be comparable to reveal gaps and inconsistencies; incomplete sources should be flagged, assumptions recorded, unresolved items marked visible, and conflicting items captured rather than discarded; analysis changes should be retained with who changed what and when, and optionally why.

slots.name: data_entities
slots.value: Security requirements, privacy requirements, policies, legal obligations, analyses, results, gaps, inconsistencies, assumptions, unresolved items, conflicts, exceptions, partial analyses, role/access information, change history records, timestamps, change reasons, and version comparison data.

slots.name: constraints
slots.value: Role-based access control is required to protect sensitive information; traceability must not be lost when connecting requirements to source policies and legal obligations; incomplete, missing, or conflicting sources must be explicitly represented rather than hidden; analysis histories should preserve changes over time for accountability and review.

slots.name: quality_concerns
slots.value: Analyses should be complete, consistent, and produced efficiently; the system should support quick identification of gaps or inconsistencies, preserve clear evidence of derivation, clearly label partial or unresolved analyses, and provide enough version history to support review and accountability.

slots.name: boundary_conditions
slots.value: Handle incomplete source policies or missing legal obligations by letting analysts flag gaps, record assumptions, and mark items unresolved; handle conflicting policies or requirements by capturing both versions and highlighting the conflict for later review; handle cases where traceability cannot be established by documenting them as exceptions and allowing partial analyses to remain usable and clearly labeled as partial; preserve change history for all edits, including user, timestamp, and optional reason, and allow side-by-side comparison of earlier versions.

slots.name: analysis_versioning
slots.value: Maintain a full history of analysis changes, including who made each change, when it was made, and an optional reason; support side-by-side comparison of earlier versions; branching and merging are possible future enhancements but are not required for day one.

slots.name: information_classification
slots.value: Sensitive material may have limited visibility while in draft or pending state; access should vary by role so only appropriate users can see or edit protected information.

slots.name: notification_and_review_workflow
slots.value: Changes should be saved immediately but may remain in a draft or pending state until review; peer review is the normal path, project managers handle higher-risk or contentious changes, and administrators handle access or system-level issues; the exact approval rule depends on project configuration.

slots.name: import_export_interoperability
slots.value: SPRAT should import from common document sources, spreadsheets, structured exports from other requirements tools, and possibly upstream policy or compliance repositories; exact systems are not yet narrowed down.

slots.name: change_review_approval
slots.value: Most edits should be reviewed before being considered final; peer review is the default approval path, with project managers involved for higher-risk or contentious changes and administrators for access or system-level issues; approval behavior is configurable by project.

slots.name: version_diff_granularity
slots.value: Side-by-side comparison of earlier versions should highlight differences in goals, requirements, trace links, scenarios, policy links, and version references where available.

slots.name: audit_retention_policy
slots.value: Approval decisions and change history should be recorded and preserved in history for audit and comparison; no specific retention duration was stated.

slots.name: draft_state_management
slots.value: Items in draft or pending state can still be edited by the creating analyst, who may also withdraw or revise them before review. Other analysts and project managers can see that the item exists, but visibility may be limited if it contains sensitive material or has not been approved yet. Finalization occurs only after required reviewer sign-off, which is recorded in history. Once final, edits create a new revision rather than overwriting the approved version.

slots.name: project_configurable_approval_rules
slots.value: Approval rules depend on the project’s configuration; most edits use peer review, while project managers handle higher-risk or contentious changes and administrators handle access or system-level issues.

slots.name: review_state_transitions
slots.value: An item moves from draft or pending to reviewed or final only after required reviewer sign-off. The approval is recorded in history, and once final, later edits create a new revision instead of overwriting the approved version.

slots.name: draft_visibility_controls
slots.value: Drafts should usually expose existence, ownership, rough subject, review status, and basic metadata to users with project access, but hide full content until approved or explicitly shared; project managers and assigned reviewers should see more detail than general analysts; guests should generally see nothing about drafts unless explicitly allowed; if an item is sensitive, even metadata may be restricted to the author, reviewers, and admins.

slots.name: sensitive_item_disclosure_rules
slots.value: Sensitive items may need metadata and content visibility limited to the author, reviewers, and admins; content should remain hidden until approved or explicitly shared, and disclosure should vary by role.

slots.name: pending_item_view_permissions
slots.value: The creating analyst can edit pending items and withdraw or revise them before review; project managers and assigned reviewers can see more detail than general analysts; guests should not see drafts unless explicitly allowed; sensitive pending items may restrict even metadata to the author, reviewers, and admins.

slots.name: import_sources
slots.value: Common document sources, spreadsheets, structured exports from other requirements tools, and upstream policy or compliance repositories.

slots.name: supported_exchange_formats
slots.value: Not yet narrowed down; source formats may require mapping into SPRAT.

slots.name: traceability_preservation_on_import_export
slots.value: Imported content should preserve the structure of the analysis, including goals, scenarios, requirements, policy links, traceability, classifications, tags, and version references where possible; mapping may be needed if source formats do not match SPRAT exactly.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder explicitly wants full change history, side-by-side version comparison, and visibility into who changed what and when, but treats branching and merging as future enhancements rather than day-one needs.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This suggests the primary operational need is auditability and reviewability, not full collaborative source-control semantics; teams likely need to explain and validate analysis evolution for accountability and compliance, while avoiding the complexity of version-control workflows until collaboration patterns justify them.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder wants changes to be saved immediately but not always treated as final, with a draft or pending state until review, and says the exact approval rule depends on project configuration.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This suggests SPRAT must support a configurable governance model that separates persistence from approval status so teams can avoid data loss while enforcing project-specific review gates for compliance, traceability, and risk control.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder says that draft or pending items may still be visible to other analysts and project managers, but visibility can be limited if the item is sensitive or has not been approved yet.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This suggests SPRAT needs a more nuanced visibility and disclosure model than simple role-based access control, likely because teams need to collaborate on in-progress analysis while still preventing premature exposure of sensitive or unvetted content.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder introduced import/export interoperability as a current slot, but no corresponding details exist yet about what external formats, source systems, or exchange constraints SPRAT must support.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely indicates analysts need to bring policies, requirements, and traceability data into and out of SPRAT from other tools or repositories, so interoperability must preserve structure, trace links, and possibly auditability when exchanging data rather than just moving plain text.
